The extreme drought (D3) category, which began in late August and expanded in September, expanded further in October to include all of the Tohono O'odham Nation and all of Santa Cruz and Cochise counties, except for the Huachuca Mountains. Extreme drought continued across all of southeast Arizona north and east of these locations and the exceptional drought (D4) category began in eastern portions of Pima and Pinal counties and western Graham County. Tucson recorded its fifth warmest October on record and while most of October was dry and warmer than normal, Tucson actually recorded its 4th earliest fall freeze on record, which was brought on by an early season winter storm that also produced low elevation snow during the last week of the month. Nevertheless, precipitation totals from this storm were generally less than a quarter inch in the valleys with around a half inch for the Mogollon Rim and some of the sky islands, and at less than 30 percent of normal precipitation for the month, were not enough to stop drought conditions from deteriorating further. The lightning-caused Cow Canyon Fire, that started in August, continued to spread in Greenlee County, consuming over 35,000 acres due to hot, dry and breezy conditions before being slowed by the early season snow. Meanwhile, several human caused wildfires took hold during October.  The largest was the Encinos Fire which consumed nearly 15,000 acres along and east of the Baboquivari Mountains in Pima County. Soil moisture readings remained  well below normal, falling to below the 5th percentile ranking in most areas, while remaining just below the 10th percentile ranking near the New Mexico state line. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell to less than 3 percent of storage capacity by the end of the month.

The fire consumed a total of 14,905 acres before becoming fully contained October 26th.  Fire suppression costs tallied $438,000.

The extreme drought (D3) category, which began in late August, continued throughout September across the same sections of southeast Arizona from Tucson north and east, and expanded southward to encompass all of Graham and Greenlee counties along with all but the southwest quarter of Cochise County. The area included the San Carlos Apache Tribe lands, the White Mountains, Pinaleno Mountains, Santa Catalina Mountains and the Chiricahua Mountains. ||Aside from isolated thunderstorms that produced heavy rain near the Pima/Cochise county line on the 8th and in northeast Cochise County on the 9th, most of the area received less than 0.25 of rainfall during September, and record breaking heat continued. While the heavy rain on the 8th doused the relatively small Spud Rock Fire in the Rincon Mountains, several other lightning caused wildfires that started in August continued into September due to the lack of monsoon rainfall. This included the Cow Canyon Fire in Greenlee County, which grew to over 1500 acres toward the end of the month in hot, dry and breezy conditions. Soil moisture readings were well below normal and fell below the 10th percentile ranking and levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell to less than 5 percent of storage capacity by the end of the month.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during January, with the exception of western Pima County. Precipitation totals for the month totaled 0.5 to 1.5 inches, with higher amounts in the form of snow on the highest mountains. These totals were 25 to 125 percent of normal, but even where substantial precipitation occurred, were not enough to improve the drought status. Soil moisture readings improved slightly, but were still below the 5th percentile ranking across Santa Cruz and eastern sections of Pima and Pinal counties and below the 10th percentile ranking elsewhere. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained around 2 percent of storage capacity.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during April, with the exception of western Pima County. |Precipitation totals for the month totaled less than 0.25 inch, or less than 25 percent of normal, in most areas, but a few locations from the Mogollon Rim across western Graham/eastern Pinal counties into east central Pima County received between 0.25 and 0.75 inch of rain. Soil moisture readings remained very low, below the 5th percentile ranking across Santa Cruz, eastern Pima and Pinal and western Graham counties and below the 10th percentile ranking elsewhere. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell close to zero percent of capacity with only 50 acre-feet--the lowest level in more than a decade. At least a dozen small wild land fires occurred during the month, three of which  grew to over 1000 acres due to dry conditions and gusty winds.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during February, with the exception of western Pima County. Precipitation totals for the month totaled 0.5 to 2.0 inches near the Mogollon Rim or 50 to 100 percent of normal, but less than a half inch elsewhere, or zero to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture readings remained very low, below the 5th percentile ranking across eastern Pinal and western Graham counties and below the 10th percentile ranking elsewhere. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained around 2 percent of storage capacity. More than a dozen small wild land fires occurred during the month, but all were quickly suppressed.

Rain and snow showers created slippery roads in parts of eastern Pima County, which led to numerous, mainly minor, traffic accidents along Interstate 19 near Green Valley and Sahuarita and along Interstate 10 in the northwest Tucson Metro area.  One accident on I-10 near the Cochise County line resulted in a rollover, which caused one east bound lane to be closed for an hour. No injuries were reported.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during March, with the exception of western Pima County. Precipitation totals for the month totaled 0.5 to 1.5 inches in some areas or 75 to 125 percent of normal, but many areas only received between 0.1 and 0.5 inch, or 15 to 75 percent of normal. Soil moisture readings remained very low, below the 5th percentile ranking across Santa Cruz, eastern Pima and Pinal and western Graham counties and below the 10th percentile ranking elsewhere. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell to less than 1 percent of storage capacity. Around 20 small wild land fires occurred during the month, but all were quickly suppressed.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during May, with the exception of western Pima County. Rain for the month totaled less than 0.10 inch in most areas with spotty amounts of 0.25 to 0.50 inch on May 20-21. Showers on May 14 only produced light rain, but gusty winds produced blowing dust from Willcox to San Simon. Soil moisture readings remained below the 5th percentile ranking, except around the 10th percentile ranking in Greenlee and southeast Graham counties. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained near zero percent of capacity.  At least two dozen small wild land fires occurred during the month, one of which, the Zacattack fire, caused the evacuation of 30 homes in Old Bisbee's Brewery Gulch, but no damage.  Three wildfires--Sycamore Canyon, Warren and Warsaw--grew to around or over 1000 acres.

Very hot high temperatures of 106 to 119 degrees, or 8 to 13 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower elevations of southeast Arizona June 12-20, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. New record daily high temperature records were established at numerous sites on several days during this period. For Tucson International Airport, this nine day period contributed to the hottest June on record and the 4th hottest temperature on record of 115 degrees occurred on June 15.  Sites that tied or broke all time hottest temperature records included Ajo with 119 degrees, Sasabe with 113, Green Valley with 112. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for 14 people found in the desert of Pima and Santa Cruz counties during this time period.

Very hot high temperatures of 106 to 119 degrees, or 8 to 13 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower elevations of southeast Arizona June 12-20, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. New record daily high temperature records were established at numerous sites on several days during this period. Lightning struck and damaged a block wall near Snyder and Sabino Canyon Rds.
A wind gust to 66 mph was measured near Old Spanish Trail and Freeman Rd.
Lightning started a roof fire in a house near Sahuarita and Wentworth Rds.
Thunderstorm winds damaged or uprooted 35 shallow-rooted trees at Evergreen Cemetery in Tucson.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during June, with the exception of western Pima County.  Most areas only tallied 0.5 or less for the month, which is close to normal. A few locations received 1-1.5 of rain, but that was not enough to make up for record rainfall deficits over the past 12 to 15 months. Soil moisture readings remained below the 5th percentile ranking across most of southeast Arizona except around the 10th percentile ranking in Greenlee and southeast Graham counties. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained near zero percent of capacity. Numerous human and lightning caused wild land fires occurred, five of which grew to more than 10,000 acres during the hot, dry and windy month.
Photo showed a landspout in northeast Tucson around Skyline and Kolb. No damage occurred.
A storm chaser observed a funnel cloud for 3 minutes in northeast Tucson around Swan and Sunrise.
Thunderstorm winds blew a metal utility shed into a utility pole at Magee Rd. and La Ca��ada Dr.

Hot temperatures, 5 to 10 degrees above normal, were experienced on June 6-7 with high temperatures in the upper 90s to 100 degrees, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for three males found in the desert, one on the Tohono O'odham Nation near Vamori, one near Arivaca, and another north of Amado.

A wet July caused the exceptional (D4) drought category and extreme (D3) drought category to cease across nearly all of southeast Arizona, with exceptional drought only remaining in far southeast Cochise County by the end of the month. The extreme (D3) drought category remained across the rest of eastern and central Cochise County, much of Graham and Greenlee counties and parts of the Tohono O'odham Nation. July rainfall varied widely from 2 to 15 inches across southeast Arizona. In areas where the drought lingered through the end of the month this equated to 75 to 125 percent of normal rainfall while areas in which the drought eased further rainfall tallied as much as 400 percent of normal. July ranked as the wettest on record for any month at the Tucson International Airport where 8.06 inches was recorded. The rainfall caused wildfire season to end and soil moisture readings to improve from below the 10th percentile to between the 30th and 70th percentiles by month's end. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir started to rise, but only reached slightly more than 1 percent of capacity by the end of the month.
A wind gust to 67 mph was recorded at Tucson International Airport.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to two homes in Anegam and substantial damage to a home in Comobabi.
Lightning struck a house on N Sweet Heather Way in Green Valley causing a small attic fire, which was quickly extinguished.

Thunderstorm winds downed 60 power poles and numerous trees and in Green Valley and Sahuarita, mostly along La Canada Dr. from Duval Mine Rd to near Anamax Rd. and near the entrance to Quail Creek. A traffic signal was also damaged in Green Valley while the wall of a townhouse was blown over in Sahuarita.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near Interstate 10 and Houghton.

One to two inches of rain fell in less than 1 hour northeast of the Tucson International Airport causing flash flooding of area roads. One swift water rescue was conducted for a vehicle stalled in a wash.
Thunderstorm wind gusts downed several trees in western Oro Valley and Marana and downed power poles along Trico Rd.
Thunderstorm outflow winds produced widespread blowing dust that reduced visibilities to less than a quarter mile from Green Valley to Marana causing traffic disruptions along Interstates 19 and 10.

Heavy rain of 2.5 in less than 90 minutes occurred near the headwaters of Rincon Creek. Flash flooding occurred downstream in the Rincon Ranch Estates area. Camino Loma Alta became flooded and impassible.

Around 2.5 of rain in less than 1 hour was measured near the headwaters of Sabino Creek in the Bighorn burn scar and caused a two-foot rise in the stream that crosses trails in the Sabino Canyon Recreation Area. Six hikers had to be rescued after becoming trapped by the high flows.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole near Nolic.

Widespread heavy rain across eastern Pima County resulted in widespread flooding of roadways and high flows along Pantano Wash and Rillito River. Significant damage to the Loop hiking and biking trail system occurred.

Thunderstorms winds downed 30 power poles and dozens of trees in Green Valley and Sahuarita. One of the downed trees broke a water main and other blocked streets. Around 10,000 customers were without power into the overnight hours. A CoCoRaHS observer on the southeast side of Green Valley measured a wind gust of 66 mph at 1855MST.
Heavy rain of 2.5 in less than 1 hour at the headwaters of Tanque Verde Creek caused a 1 foot rise in water levels at Tanque Verde Loop Road, resulting in its closure.

Between 1 and 1.5 of rain fell in less than 1 hour in central Tucson causing widespread street flooding with water flowing across roads 1 to 2 feet deep. Swift water rescues occurred near the intersections of Grant and Tucson and Silverlake and Euclid with vehicles stranded at Mabel and 7th Ave. and the Orange Grove/I-10 underpass.  A house was flooded near Speedway and Country Club.

Between 1 and 1.5 of rain fell in less than 1 hour south and west of the Tucson Mountains to near Three Points causing widespread street flooding and street closures due to water flowing across roads 1 to 2 feet deep. A vehicle was stranded in flood waters at the intersection of Snyder Hill and Sandario. Several dirt roads were washed out in the Three Points area.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near the intersection of Speedway and Craycroft, which led to a traffic accident.

A large area of 1 to 2 of rain fell in less than 90 minutes in southeast Pima County and caused extensive flash flooding from southeast Tucson and Vail southwest to Sahuarita and Green Valley. In the Vail area, three to four feet of water washed out East Andrada Rd at the Santa Rita Wash and a car was swept downstream 300 yards, but the occupants escaped unharmed.  Many roads in Saguaro National Park East were also flooded or closed.  In southeast Tucson, a person was rescued from a sandbar in the Pantano Wash near Harrison Rd. and farther south, Sahuarita and Wilmot Rds. were closed. In Sahuarita a woman was rescued from her vehicle at Beta Street and the Interstate 19 Frontage Rd.  In Green Valley, several roads were closed and homes were flooded in the Casa de Abrego neighborhood east of I-19.

Thunderstorm winds caused damage at a church complex near Broadway and Craycroft in Tucson, blowing in one 50-foot tall stained glass window and blowing out another.  An awning was damaged on the school building and the pastor's residence suffered shingle damage.  A tree was also downed which damaged an iron post fence, and the church marquis was damaged. Nearby, a tree was downed damaging the wall of a house. Several other trees were downed farther north and west and a carport was destroyed near 5th St. and Alvernon Way.
Thunderstorm winds downed more than a dozen large trees at an apartment complex near Orange Grove and Oracle Rds. The downed trees fell on carports and vehicles, and destroyed an apartment stairwell.
One hour rainfall of 0.5 to 1 on ground saturated from rain the previous day caused flash flooding northeast of Ryan Field and the closure of Snyder Hill Rd west of San Joaquin Rd.
Two inches of rain in 2 hours north of Three Points caused flooding of roadways west of Picture Rocks. A vehicle was stranded in floodwaters on Tucker Road at the Blanco Wash.
Heavy rain of 2 to 3.5 in 90 minutes caused flash flooding of washes and the closure of many roadways in Green Valley.

Heavy rain of 1 to 1.5 in less than 1 hour fell in Green Valley and caused flash flooding and the closure of several roads. Five homes were flooded in the Casa de Abrego neighborhood, some of which had just been flooded less than 48 hours earlier.
Two to four inches of rain in 90 minutes caused flash flooding of washes up to 3 feet deep across Arivaca Rd. prompting its closure.
Heavy rain of 1.5 in less than one hour near Kohatk resulted in minor flooding of two homes in that village.
Two inches of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding across Highway 86 near Indian Route 26 northwest of Sells.

A large area of two inches of rain occurred in three hours in east Tucson, generally east of Craycroft Rd. to the Rincon Mts. with more than 4 inches of rain from Broadway and Wilmot to Tanque Verde and Pantano Rds.  Numerous roads were flooded or damaged including Pima Rd. and Robb Wash. Several swift water rescues of motorists occurred including one vehicle washed downstream near Camino Loma Alta and Old Spanish Trail. Alamo Wash left its banks and flooded several homes between Pima and Speedway.
A wind gust to 63 mph was recorded at the Empire RAWS.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles near the intersection of Speedway and Painted Hills.

Heavy rain of 1 to 1.5 in 90 minutes west of Interstate 10 and north of Highway 86 in Tucson resulted in flash flooding and the closure of several roads including Bopp Rd, Jamie Ave, Aldon Rd, and Sandario Rd. A vehicle was stranded in floodwaters at Sweetwater and Silverbell.

Strong flows continued in the Canada Del Oro Wash as a result of 1 to 2 of rain in less than an hour in the upper reaches of the basin within the Bighorn burn scar. Overton Rd. was closed due to flooding and the loop trail at Christina Taylor Green Park was flooded. More than an inch of rain in less than 1 hour also occurred from Marana to the southern Tortolita Mountains. As a result a swift water rescue was performed near Grier and Sandario and another west of Edwin and Oracle Rds.
Heavy rain of 2.5 in less than 1 hour at the headwaters of Tanque Verde Creek caused rapid rises of over three feet in Tanque Verde Creek downstream before the channel widens out.

Two to four inches of rain in less than two hours over the Bighorn burn scar area in the Santa Catalina Mountains caused flash flooding of several washes and roadways.  Sutherland Wash rose over 5 feet at a gauge just east of Oro Valley and the Canada del Oro Wash also rose, especially downstream of its confluence with the Sutherland Wash. Downstream flash flooding resulted at Overton Rd where 5 people were rescued from two different vehicles which were swept downstream.

Over one inch of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding in Sabino Canyon Recreation area and the closure of roadways. Several hikers were stranded and needed to be rescued after floodwaters rose.
One inch of rain in less than 1 hour in Catalina Foothills caused flash flooding of River Rd. near Pontatoc Rd.
Two inches of rain caused the ceiling to collapse in an apartment complex near 22nd and Craycroft. Twelve apartments sustained damage.
Two inches of rain in less than 1 hour caused extensive flooding of Arivaca Road between mile markers 10 and 16 with additional flash flooding farther north near Keystone Peak.
The Sasabe RAWS measured a wind gust of 66 mph.
Thunderstorm winds destroyed a dwelling at Cold Fields.

More than 1 inch of rain in less than 1 hour fell along State Route 286 north of Santa Margarita Road west to the Baboquivari Mountains causing a number of washes to flow east across Route 286 two to three feet deep.
Heavy rain of 1 to 2 in 90 minutes caused flash flooding in rural areas west of Green Valley. Mission Rd. north of Duval Mine Rd. was closed.
One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour from south of Ajo to east of Why. This caused flash flooding of area washes and the closure of Highway 86 east of Why and Highway 85 between Ajo and Why.
Three hour rainfall of 2.5 fell at the headwaters of Rincon Creek, causing rapid rises in stream flow and flash flooding of Old Spanish Trail.

A broad area of 1.5 of rain, with pockets of 3 to 4, fell in less than 90 minutes and caused numerous road closures from Picture Rocks to Saguaro National Park West to southeast of Three Points. Kinney Rd. near Sonora Desert Museum was one of the major roads that was closed due to flooding.
Early morning rainfall of 1 to 1.5 on saturated ground quickly resulted in flash flooding and closure of several roads in north Marana.
More than 1 of rain fell on saturated ground causing flash flooding of several roadways from Sahuarita to Corona De Tucson, including Sahuarita Rd. near Wilmot Rd.

One to two inches of rain on saturated ground cause numerous flooded and closed roads in the Vail area from just east of Rita Ranch to Old Spanish Trail and south to near Interstate 10. One vehicle was stuck in floodwaters near Old Spanish Trail and Drexel Rd.
More than 1 of rain fell in less than 1 hour along South Wilmot Rd causing flash flooding and the closure of the roadway north of Sahuarita Rd.

Heavy rain of 1 to 2 in less than an hour in the upper reaches of the Canada Del Oro Wash within the Bighorn burn scar caused rapid rises downstream. Rail North Rd along Lago Del Oro Parkway to Wilds Rd was closed to high water levels.
Heavy rain of 1 to 1.5 fell in less that 1 hour in the Catalina Foothills. Ventana Wash rose and flowed up to 18 deep across Snyder Rd, causing its closure.
Heavy rain of 1-2 in less than 1 hour from Tucson Mt Park to Highway 86 caused the flooding and closure of Bopp Rd closed in several locations from Lead Flower Ave west past San Joaquin Rd.
Heavy rain of 2 to 3 in less than 1 hour at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument caused flash flooding of roadways making them impassible.

One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour over east central Tucson caused flash flooding along and near Alamo Wash.  A child was rescued from flood waters near 22nd and Kolb.  Farther north, Alamo Wash overtopped Speedway Blvd and Sahuara Ave.
A wind gust to 60 mph was recorded at Tucson International Airport at 1904MST. Outflow winds downed trees in midtown Tucson and in Marana.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles near Speedway Blvd and Tanque Verde Loop Rd. A private weather station near Escalante and Freeman Roads measured a gust to 76 mph at 1943MST.

Thunderstorm winds downed multiple trees in eastern Tucson. A wind gust to 64 mph was recorded at Davis-Monthan AFB at 1946MST and a gust to 58 mph was recorded at a private weather station near Irvington and Harrison at 1948MST.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to a house in Little Tucson on the Tohono O'odham Nation.
Thunderstorm winds downed three power poles north of the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument Visitor Center.

One inch of rain in 15 to 30 minutes created flash flooding of washes and roadways in a small portion of east Tucson. A vehicle was stranded in flowing water near 5th St. and Wilmot Rd. Flood waters also crossed roadways in Wilshire Heights near Broadway and Craycroft.

Thunderstorm winds several downed trees and power poles between Campbell Ave. and Palo Verde Rd. and between Drexel and Irvington Rds. About 2000 customers were without power and a section of Irvington Rd. was closed as a result. Tents at Community Food Bank were blown down causing closure of outdoor food distribution operations the following 2 days.

Up to three inches of rain west and northwest of Tucson late in the evening caused flash flooding of Brawley Wash and smaller washes that flow into it.  An additional one to two inches of rainfall during the predawn hours south of Three Points flowed through the Altar Wash into the Brawley Wash causing flooding along it from northeast of Three Points through the Garcia Strip of the Tohono O'odham Nation, north to Marana from early that morning into late afternoon. Damage to area roads resulted.
More than 1 of rain in less than 1 hour in Vail caused flash flooding of roadways including Old Vail Rd. and Dawn Rd.
More than 1 inch of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding in central and eastern Tucson. This includes roadways near the intersections of Speedway and Swan and Grant and 1st Ave.

A broad area of 1 to 2 of rain fell in less than 1 hour from the Tucson Mountains west to Picture Rocks. Numerous streets were flooded, closed and/or damaged as a result. At least one vehicle was stranded in flood waters, on Manville Rd.
Up to 1 of rain on saturated ground caused Franco Wash to rise rapidly and flood and damage several roads in the Summit area.

More than one inch of rain in less than an hour caused a rapid rise in Alamo Wash where a storm had produced an inch of rain three hours earlier.  A motorist was rescued from a vehicle stuck in floodwaters on Chantilly Rd. at the Alamo Wash.
Thunderstorms winds downed two power poles in Catalina at Highway 77 near Graham Rd.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees along Dove Mountain Blvd. north of Moore Rd.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees near the intersection of Ina and Oracle Rds.

Temperatures 5 degrees above normal near 110 degrees, occurred in western Pima County causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached on July 6. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male found in the desert west of Ajo.

Thunderstorm winds downed or uprooted numerous trees in midtown Tucson including several at a cemetery on Prince Rd and Oracle Blvd. One tree fell on a house near Pima St. and Columbus Blvd. and another damaged a car at River Rd. and 1st Ave. Winds also damaged a house under construction near Prince and Country Club Rd. and downed large |power poles near Tucson Mall causing the closure of 1st Ave between River and Wetmore Rds. About 6000 customers lost electricity service.

A large area of 1 to 3 of rain fell in less than 1 hour over much of the Tucson Metro Area, including parts of the Bighorn burn scar. Around ten swift water rescues were performed during the overnight hours for motorists trapped in vehicles including near Escalante and Sarnoff. Plus, two people were rescued from the Rillito River near La Canada Dr. Also, many trails were damaged at Sabino Canyon Recreation Area and six homes were flooded in near Finger Rock Wash in the Catalina Foothills due to runoff from the Bighorn burn scar. No injuries were reported.

Very hot high temperatures of 101 to 107 degrees, or 8 to 12 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower elevations of Graham and eastern sections of Pinal and Pima counties on August 4, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. High temperatures included 107 degrees at Tucson International Airport, 102 at Safford Airport, and 101 at Green Valley, San Manuel and Duncan. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one person found in the desert near Three Points.
More than 1.5 of rain in 3 hours caused the Artesia Wash to flow swiftly and to flood Highway 86 west of Sells.

Very hot high temperatures of 104 to 114 degrees, or 5 to 11 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower elevations of Pima, southeast Pinal, and northwest sections of Cochise and Graham counties August 25-27 and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. The highest temperatures at select locations during the period were 114 degrees (tied record on 8/27) at Ajo, 112 (both records on 8/26 and 8/27) at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, 111 (record on 8/26) at Sells, 108 (one degree shy of the record on 8/27) at Picacho, 106 on 8/26 at Tucson International Airport, 105 on 8/25 and 8/26 at San Carlos and 103 on 8/25 at Cascabel.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole at Dawn and Houghton Rds. in Vail.

More than 1 inch of rain in an hour caused flash flooding in northeast Tucson. Flash flooding was reported along Castle Rock Wash and one vehicle was stranded in flood waters near Bear Canyon and Tanque Verde Rds. Fort Lowell Rd. was closed due to flooding.

Very hot high temperatures of 104 to 115 degrees, or 8 to 12 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower deserts of Pima and Pinal counties August 3-4, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. High temperatures on August 3 included 115 degrees at Ajo (record), 109 at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, 108 at Sells, and 104 at Picacho. On August 4 highs included 115 degrees at Ajo (tie), 110 at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, 109 at Sells (record), and 107 at Picacho. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one person found in the desert near San Miguel.

Very hot high temperatures of 104 to 114 degrees, or 5 to 11 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower elevations of Pima, southeast Pinal, and northwest sections of Cochise and Graham counties August 25-27 and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. The highest temperatures at select locations during the period were 114 degrees (tied record on 8/27) at Ajo, 112 (both records on 8/26 and 8/27) at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, 111 (record on 8/26) at Sells, 108 (one degree shy of the record on 8/27) at Picacho, 106 on 8/26 at Tucson International Airport, 105 on 8/25 and 8/26 at San Carlos and 103 on 8/25 at Cascabel.
One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour caused flash flooding of washes across roadways in northeast Tucson. One vehicle became stranded in floodwaters near Tanque Verde Rd and Conestoga Ave.
Lightning struck a water heater at one home starting a fire, and caused damage to an adjacent house near Sweetwater and Silverbell Dr. in west Tucson.

Thunderstorm winds uprooted trees at Forty Niner Country Club and downed trees blocked roadways near the intersections of Old Spanish Trail and Houghton as well as Golf Links and Harrison. A wind gust of 79 mph was measured on Larkspur Rd.
Thunderstorm winds downed large branches along Woodland Rd. in northeast Tucson.

Another 1 to 2 of heavy rain in less than an hour with a 3-hour total of 2 to 4 caused additional flash flooding of washes and roadways on Tucson's northeast side. Three people were rescued when their vehicle was swept down Bonanza Wash near Bonanza Ave. and E Forest Grove Loop.
Scout Camp RAWS measured a thunderstorm wind gust to 64 mph.
One to two inches of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding in Picture Rocks. Manville Rd. was closed due to flooding at the Brawley Wash and Sandario Rd. was also closed.

Two to three inches of rain in 2 hours along and south of Highway 86 caused flash flooding south of Ryan Field Airport and around Tucson Mountain Park Estates. Sierrita Mt. Rd. was closed near Hilltop Rd. and both Sandario Rd. and Snyder Hill Rd. was closed at the Black Wash.

One to two inches of rain in two hours caused flash flooding in Marana and Avra Valley. Anway Rd. was closed south of El Camino de Tres Arroyos as well as Silverbell Rd. near the Cocio Wash. Avra Valley Rd. was closed at the Brawley Wash.
A severe wind gust was measured by a Pima County weather station located at the KEMX radar site.

Very hot high temperatures around 10 degrees above normal occurred across the lower elevations of southeast Arizona on July 22, causing the High Heat Risk category to be reached. The hottest temperature was 112 at Ajo. Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, Sells, Picacho, and Safford Airport (record) all topped out at 108 degrees.  Tucson International Airport reached 107.

Heavy rain of 1.5-2.5 fell in less than 1 hour over the Finger Rock Canyon watershed with 2.29 recorded in 30 minutes at the Mt. Kimball gauge near the headwaters, which was in the severe burn area of the 2020 Bighorn Fire burn scar. Finger Rock Wash rose over 14 feet at a downstream gauge at the mouth of the canyon. Residents of seven homes and 12 people from another which was used as an assisted living facility were evacuated due to as much as 3 feet of water inside the structures.  Most of the structures will be purchased by the county and torn down. Several of the roads in the area were washed out and the wash structure itself was damaged.
Scout Camp RAWS measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph.

Heavy rain of 1-1.5 in less than 1 hour in the Broadway/Alvernon area led to rises in Arroyo Chico Wash. Crossings at Plumer Ave. and others were impassable. Additionally, a man on foot was swept away near 6th St. and 9th Ave.  He was rescued, but sustained minor injuries.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted trees near Greenock and Oracle Rd. in Oro Valley.
Heavy rain of 1-2 in less than 1 hour near Tucson Mountain Park, caused flash flooding of several roads in Tucson Estates. Sheridan Ave. was washed out south of Kinney.
Lightning struck at house on Calle del Escribo in Sahuarita causing extensive damage.  The owner of the house was treated for 2nd degree burns, which resulted from the fire.
Heavy rain of 2-3 in 90 minutes caused a rapid rise in Canada Del Oro Wash, causing the flooding and closure of Overton Rd.
Heavy rain of 3-4 in 90 minutes caused flash flooding of Highway 85 near Puerto Blanco Dr. north of Lukeville.
Heavy rain of around 3 in 2 hours caused flash flooding of Highway 86 southeast of the Gu-Achi Trading Post. Santa Rosa Wash rose several feet north of Highway 86 but remained within its banks.
Ping pong size hail buffeted Green Valley for several minutes. Numerous sky lights were damaged and several houses suffered broken windows.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a road sign near the Continental exit of Interstate 19 and 100 trees were downed in Green Valley.
Thunderstorm winds downed power lines near Drexel and Calle Santa Cruz and downed large tree branches near Snyder and Bear Canyon Rds.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree near Tangerine and Lon Adams Rds.
Around 1 of heavy rain in less an 1 hour caused Valley View Wash to flood N. Flecha Dr. as well as River Rd. between Swan and Pontatoc Rds. in the Catalina Foothils.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole south of Pisinemo near the junction of Routes 21 and 24.
Quarter to ping pong size hail fell across Tucson from Bilby and Houghton to Davis-Monthan AFB.
Thunderstorm winds downed a few trees in Midvale Park in the southwest Tucson metro area. One of the trees fell onto a residence, causing minor damage.

Heavy rain of 1-2 in 1 hour caused flash flooding of roadways in southeast Tucson. Road closures included Wilmot Rd. north of Noyes, Escalante Rd. at Atterbury Wash and Harrison Rd. at the Pantano Wash.

Hot high temperatures around 105 degrees, or 5 degrees above normal, occurred on July 17 and 18, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found outdoors in Tucson on the 17th and another found in the desert near Three Points on the 18th.

Hot high temperatures between 105 and 107, or 5 to 7 degrees above normal, occurred on July 14, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for two individuals found outdoors in Tucson.

Hot high temperatures between 105 and 107, or 5 to 7 degrees above normal, occurred on July 8 and 9, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found outdoors in Tucson on the 9th. Heat was found to be a contributing factor for another individual found outdoors in Tucson on the 8th. Epilepsy was a complicating factor in that fatality.
A thunderstorms outflow gust to 60 mph was measured at KTUS at 2110MST. A thunderstorm gust 60 mph was measured in east Tucson at 2123MST.
Strong winds blew down a 20-year old Acacia tree in Oro Valley.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted a tree near 6th St. and 6th Ave. in Tucson. The tree fell on top of a parked car.
Heavy rain of 1.5 in 1 hour caused flash flooding and the closure of Camino Verde Rd. near Bilby.
Thunderstorm winds downed tree near 5th St. and Freeman Rd.

Hot temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above normal, near 90 degrees, were experienced in southeast Pima County on March 26 causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be approached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male found in the desert seven miles southeast of Green Valley.

Temperatures in the upper 20 to lower 30s were observed during the early morning hours of February 24, and were preceded by a quarter inch of rain that fell on the 23rd. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that hypothermia was the primary cause of death for one adult male in the desert in the Ironwood National Forest northwest of Tucson.

Heavy rain of 1-2 in 90 minutes caused flash flooding of roadways from southeast to north central Tucson. Road closures included Escalante at Atterbury Wash, Harrison and Pantano Wash, Old Spanish Trail and Freeman Road, Bears Path Rd. south of Tanque Verde Road and Rudasill at Pima Wash.
Heavy rain of 2-3 in 90 minutes caused Gunsight Wash to rise rapidly and flood/close Highway 85 near mile post 55.

Very hot high temperatures around 10 degrees above normal occurred across the lower elevations of southeast Arizona on July 22, causing the High Heat Risk category to be reached. The hottest temperature was 112 at Ajo. Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, Sells, Picacho, and Safford Airport (record) all topped out at 108 degrees.  Tucson International Airport reached 107.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power line near Kenyon Dr and Gollob Rd.
Thunderstorms winds downed large limbs of several trees.
Nearly 1.5 of rain in 30 minutes on the Empire Mountains washed out Hilton Ranch Rd. which leads to the KEMX radar.
Thunderstorm winds downed multiple trees near Cortaro and Thornydale Rds. and downed power poles along Linda Vista Blvd.
Heavy rain of 1-2 in 1 hour caused flash flooding and the closure of Tangerine Rd. between Interstate 10 and Twin Peaks Rd.

Hot high temperatures between 101 and 103, or 2 to 4 degrees above normal, occurred on August 16, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for two elderly individuals found in their Tucson homes.
Heavy rain of 1.5-2.5 in 90 minutes caused flash flooding and road closures in Picture Rocks.  A school bus became stuck in floodwaters at Ina and Sandario Rds.
Heavy rain of 1.5-2.5 caused flash flooding and road closures in southwest Tucson along Camino Verde as well as Old Ajo Hwy.
Heavy rain of 1.5-2.5 in less than 2 hours caused flash flooding in Oro Valley and the closures of Overton and Hardy Roads and Linda Vista Blvd.
Thunderstorms produced one inch of rain in less than one hour over the Contreras burn scar causing a debris flow over State Route 386 to Kitt Peak.

Hot high temperatures 101 to 103 degrees, or 3 to 5 degrees above normal, occurred on September 2 causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found in their Green Valley home.
A funnel cloud formed briefily near Diamond Bell Ranch south of Three Points, AZ.
Heavy rain of 1.5 in 1 hour caused flash flooding southeast of Three Points including Sierra Mountain Rd.

Hot high temperatures around 105 degrees, or 5 degrees above normal, occurred on July 18, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found in the desert near Three Points.
Lightning struck a power pole along Route 15 just north of Highway 86. The pole caught fire and caused a power outage on the Tohono O'odham Nation that persisted for three hours.

Very hot high temperatures nearly 10 degrees above normal occurred on June 23 with low temperatures in the lower 80s, causing the High Heat Risk category to be reached. Ajo topped out at 110 degrees and Organ Pipe National Monument reached 108. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found in the desert on the Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge.
Heavy rain of 3-4 inches in 2 hours caused flash flooding across State Route 286 and 2-3 inches of rain caused flash flooding and the closure of Sasabe-Arivaca Road at mile post 2.
Thunderstorms produced 1.5 inches of rain in one hour over the Contreras burn scar causing a debris flow over State Route 386 to Kitt Peak.
Heavy rain of an inch in one hour caused flash flooding near Agua Caliente Park and the closure of Soldier Trail Rd. near Roger Rd.

A lightning strike at Agua Caliente Park on the northeast side of the Tucson Metro area ignited a blaze that damaged 225 palm trees and 40 other trees. The fire also damaged signs, picnic tables, trash cans, a bike rack, and parts of irrigation systems. About 40 palm trees were so severely burned they were removed. The park remained closed for 60 days.

Hot temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal, between 100 and 104 degrees, were experienced in the Tucson Metro May 26-27 causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for three elderly individuals.

Very hot high temperatures occurred across western Pima and south central Pinal counties and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. Ajo and Picacho topped out at 110 degrees and Organ Pipe National Monument reached 108.
A wind gust to 76 mph was recorded at KTUS Tucson Airport ASOS at 1834MST and a gust to 64 mph was recorded there at 1753MST. No damage was observed in the immediate vicinity.
Thunderstorms winds downed 8 power poles along Mission Rd.

Two periods of heavy rain, each of 1 across much of the watershed, which was part of the Bighorn Fire burn scar, caused Sabino Creek to overtop bridges at the Sabino Canyon Recreation area. Some hiking trails, which were affected by high flows earlier in the month, sustained additional damage.
Heavy rain of 2 in 1 hour in the vicinity of Davis-Monthan AFB caused flash flooding and the closure of nearby roads including Contractors Way.
Thunderstorm wind gusts to 60 mph downed tree limbs in Green Valley.
Heavy rain of 1.5 on the Bighorn burn scar caused rapid rises in Finger Rock Wash. Road closures resulted near Havasu Rd and Columbus Blvd and Pontatoc Rd. south of Skyline Dr.
Thunderstorm wind downed 3 power poles south of North Komelik.
Heavy rain of 2 in 1 hour fell upstream to north of the Catalina Mountains in Pinal County. The Canada Del Oro Wash flowed over its banks south of Edwin Rd.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole near Highway 86 and San Pedro Rd.
Heavy rain of 1.5 in 2-3 hours caused Old Ajo Hwy. and West Snyder Hill Rd. north of Ryan Field to be closed due to flash flooding.

Very hot high temperatures of 107 to 112 degrees occurred with low temperatures in the upper 70s to lower 80s, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. Ajo set records with 111 degrees on the 10th and 112 on the 11th. Organ Pipe National Monument topped out at 109 on the 11th and 12th.
Heavy rain of 1.5 in 1 hour caused flash flooding in southern Tucson. Swift water rescues from vehicles occurred near Bilby Rd. and Nogales Highway and Valencia Rd. and Park Ave.

Very hot high temperatures occurred across Santa Cruz, eastern Pima, southeast Pinal and northwest Cochise counties and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. Tucson airport topped out at 111 degrees, Sasabe and Cascabel reached 109 while Nogales Airport and San Manuel hit 106.
Heavy rain of 1-1.5 in 90 minutes caused flash flooding in Saguaro National Park and damage to Bajada Loop Rd.
Heavy rain of 1-1.5 southeast of Valencia and Mission Rds. caused the West Branch of the Santa Cruz River to flood Drexel Road, causing its closure.
Thunderstorm winds downed multiple tree branches and downed one shallow rooted tree in a parking lot along Ina Rd between La Cholla and Oracle Rds.
Heavy rain of 1.5 to 3 inches in less than 3 hours caused flash flooding along Empire Ranch Rd.
Thunderstorms produced 2-3 inches of rain in one hour over the Contreras burn scar causing a debris flow over State Route 386 to Kitt Peak.
Thunderstorm winds downed power lines near Santa Rosa.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees near Skyline Dr. and Campbell Rd. in the Catalina Foothills.
Nearly 2 inches of rain in less than 2 hours over the Contreras burn scar caused a 1-2 ft debris flow across State Highway 386 to Kitt Peak.
Heavy rain of 3-4 in three hours caused flash flooding and road closures in Green Valley, including Camino Del Sol and Abrego Drive.
Heavy rain of 2-3 in 90 minutes caused flash flooding in southwest Tucson. Roads closed include Old Ajo Highway, Long Cast DR. and Iberia Ave.
Thunderstorm winds downed power lines on Sanders Rd. causing its closure and the lost of power for more than 2000 customers. Winds also downed several Palo Verde trees near  Moore Rd.

Very hot high temperatures around 10 degrees above normal occurred on July 11, causing the High Heat Risk category to be reached. The Tucson International Airport topped out at 110 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found in the desert south of Three Points.
Thunderstorm winds severely damaged an RV port and downed large tree limbs southwest of Mescal.
Thunderstorm outflow winds produced a wall of dust that reduced visibilities to less than a quarter mile across I-10 near the Pima/Pinal county line.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near Swan Rd. north of River Rd.

Heavy rain of more than 1 in 1 hour caused flash flooding and closures of residential streets south of Orange Grove Road between La Cholla and La Canada. Additionally, a man was rescued after becoming trapped under a bridge by floodwaters near Blacklidge and Walnut.

Very hot high temperatures around 10 degrees above normal occurred on July 10 and 11, causing the High Heat Risk category to be reached. Ajo reached 114 degrees on the 10th and broke a record high on the 11th with 115 degrees while Organ Pipe National Monument reached 109. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found outdoors in Ajo on the 10th.

Hot high temperatures 101 to 103 degrees, or 4 to 6 degrees above normal, occurred on September 6 causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was a contributing factor in the death of one individual found in their Marana home. Heart disease was a complicating factor in this fatality.
Heavy rain of 1-2' in less than 1 hour caused the flooding of Magee Rd. east of La Canada Dr. at Pegler Wash and the closure of Ina Rd. at Pima Wash east of Oracle Rd.

Heavy rain of 1-2 in less than 1 hour caused urban washes to flow over roadways from midtown to southeast Tucson. One person was washed downstream in the Columbus Wash near Blacklidge Dr. but was able to get themselves to safety. A young woman was rescued from her car which was stuck in Arcadia Wash near Pima and Rosemont. Kolb Rd. was closed between Irvington and Valencia while Irvington Rd. was closed due to flooding at the Atterbury Wash.
A landspout was spotted near the Los Reales landfill on the south side of Tucson. It was nearly stationary before it dissipated.
Heavy rain of 1-1.5 on Tucson's southeast side caused localized flash flooding. Escalante Rd. was closed at the Atterbury Wash and a man was rescued from his vehicle in the Alamo Wash at Yale Dr.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees near 6th St. and Euclid Ave. in Tucson.

Thunderstorm winds downed 38 power poles and numerous trees along Kolb Rd. between Golf Links and Escalante Rds. The road remained closed for more than 24 hours to clean up the area prior to replacing all the poles.  At least 6000 customers were left without power.

Heavy rain of 2-3 at the headwaters of Sabino Creek and Bear Canyon caused rapid rises in both streams. Flash flooding occurred at the Sabino Canyon Recreation area causing damage to trails and flooding of all recreation area bridges. Twenty five people became stranded in Bear Canyon and needed to be rescued as trails across the wash were flowing heavily and dangerously impassable. No injuries were reported.

Very hot high temperatures of 104 to 109 degrees occurred with low temperatures in the upper 70s to lower 80s, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. Tucson airport tied set records with 109 degrees on the 10th and 11th and Green Valley topped out at 107 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for seven individuals. On the 10th, two were found in the desert near Amado and two in Tucson (1 indoors and 1 outdoors). On the 11th, another was found outdoors in Tucson. On the 12th, one was found in Tucson Mountain Park west of Tucson and another indoors within the City of Tucson.
Upstream heavy rain of 1.5-2.5 in 2 hours caused Canada Del Oro Wash to flood part of N Lago Del Oro Parkway, resulting in its closure.
Heavy rain of 1.5-2.5 in 90 minutes over the Contreras Fire burn scar caused a 1-2 ft debris flow across State Highway 386 to Kitt Peak.
Heavy rain of 2-3 in 2 hours fell across the Rincon Mountains causing rises in Tanque Verde Creek that caused road closures of Wentworth Rd. and Tanque Verde Loop Rd.
Heavy rain of 1-2 in less than 2 hours over the Contreras Fire burn scar caused a 1-2 ft debris flow across State Highway 386 to Kitt Peak.
A thunderstorm wind gust to 62 mph was recorded at KTUS ASOS at 1534MST.  Winds blew the roof off a gazebo near Catalina Highway.
Thunderstorm winds downed several power poles in Tucson Estates. Wind gusts to 64 mph were measured at two CoCoRaHS sites in the Rancho Del Cerro area.
Quarter size hail broke a window and caused roof damage to residences at Tucson Estates.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles in Pisinimo and Hickiwan Districts on the Tohono O'odham Nation.
Trained spotters submitted a video of a landspout tornado. Location estimated to be in an open area near Orange Grove Road and Blanco Wash Trail.
Large hail damaged several vehicle windows near Marana High School.
Thunderstorm winds downed five power poles near Tucker and Anway Rds.
The lightning caused Soto Fire began August 7 north of Green Valley. The fire consumed 1,046 acres before containment on August 10. Fire suppression costs tallied $160,000.
The Tucson International Airport ASOS KTUS measured a gust of 62 mph at 1833MST.
A short-lived funnel cloud was photographed south of Ina and Silverbell in Marana.

Thunderstorm winds downed six power poles along Moore Rd between Frontage and Clark Farms Rds. in Marana and four poles along Avra Valley Rd. between Garvey and Trico Rds. in Picture Rocks. A wind gust to 58 mph was recorded at KMZJ Pinal Air Park AWOS.
Thunderstorm winds downed three power poles down near Kohatk.

Very hot temperatures of 7 to 11 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across eastern Pima County August 27-30. Record highs at Tucson International Airport included 109 degrees on August 28 and 108 on the 29th. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found indoors on the 28th with a nonfunctioning AC unit in Green Valley where the temperature topped out at 103 degrees. Heat was found to be a contributing factor in the death of four individuals outdoors in Tucson during the period. Two were found outdoors and also experienced a complicating factor of drug toxicity. Three had complicating factors of drug toxicity and one suffered from other health conditions.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees and damaged roofs, awnings, carports and sheds in a mobile home park near Irvington and Harrison. A gust to 76 mph was measured at CWOP site FW9797 at 2016MST.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole in the Santa Rosa area.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees on the Pascua Yaqui Pueblo.
Thunderstorm winds damage the roof of one home in Pia Oik and two in Gu Vo.
Thunderstorm winds downed 3 power poles in the San Simon, Kuakatch and Charco 27 areas.

Hot temperatures 2 to 4 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in the Tucson Metro area where temperatures topped out between 98 and 102. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined heat to be the primary cause of death for one individual who was found in the car in which he was living in southwest Tucson. Heat was found to be a contributing factor in the death of another person who died in their Oro Valley home in which the A/C unit was either broken or turned off. Heart disease was a complicating factor in this fatality.

Low temperatures in the mid to upper 20s with wind chills near 20 degrees resulted in cold that was 15 to 20 degrees below the normal low temperature for February 6. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that hypothermia was the primary cause of death for a homeless individual who had ingested methamphetamines and was found outdoors in downtown Tucson. The individual was transported to a hospital, but died later that day.

The lightning-caused Ventana Fire started before sunrise June 20 on the edge of the Tucson Metro area in the foothills of the Santa Catalina Mountains. The fire was contained by June 23 after it consumed 133 acres.

Hot temperatures 3 to 6 degrees above normal were experienced in the Tucson Metro Area June 24, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. Tucson International Airport topped out at 105 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was a contributing factor in the death of one individual found in a homeless encampment in Tucson.

Very hot temperatures 5 to 8 degrees above normal were experienced in western Pima County and the Tohono O'odham Nation June 25-26, causing the Major Heat Risk category to be reached. Ajo topped out at 112 degrees both days while Sells reached 107. On June 26, Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument topped out at 109 degrees.  The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary factor in the death of one individual found in the desert near Sells.

Very hot temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal were experienced in the Tucson Metro area June 25-27, causing the Major Heat Risk category to be reached. The Tucson International Airport reached 111 degrees on June 25-26 and 108 on June 27. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was a contributing factor in the death of one individual in Tucson found on the street on June 26.

Hot temperatures 3 to 6 degrees above normal were experienced in the Tucson Metro Area June 28-29, causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached. Tucson International Airport reached 107, 106, and 105 degrees, respectively. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was a contributing factor in the death of three individuals in Tucson. One was found in an open desert area on June 28, another in a street median on June 29, and the third in a shed next to his dwelling on June 30.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power line. The line was struck by a train, causing a power pole to fall across Aviation Highway. Winds also downed a small tree at Golf Links and Swan.

Hot temperatures 11 to 14 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in western Pima County where temperatures topped out between 100 and 105 degrees. A record high temperature of 103 degrees occurred at Ajo. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined heat to be the primary cause of death for one individual found in the desert west of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.

Hot temperatures 3 to 5 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in east central Pima County where temperatures topped out around 100 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined heat to be the primary cause of death for one individual found in the desert southwest of Three Points.

Very hot temperatures of 10 to 14 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across western Pima and southeast Pinal counties September 9-10. Record highs at Ajo were 115 and 113 degrees, respectively. Record highs at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument were 111 degrees on both days. Record highs at Picacho Peak were 109 and 110 degrees and records at San Manuel were 101 and 106 degrees.

Very hot temperatures around 10 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across the Tucson Metro area September 9-10. Record highs at Tucson International Airport were 108 and 111 degrees, respectively. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was a contributing factor in the death an elderly individual in their Tucson back yard. Heart disease was a complicating factor in this fatality.

Hot temperatures around 8 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in the Tucson Metro area where temperatures topped out around 100 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was a contributing factor in the death an individual found in a parking lot in Tucson. Heart disease was a complicating factor in this fatality.
Hail ranging from the size of quarters to golf balls fell from Speedway and Wilmot to Broadway and Campbell. There were sporadic reports of damage to car windows and skylights.

Very hot temperatures of 5 to 9 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached the first eight days of July. High temperatures at the Tucson International Airport ranged from 107 to 110 degrees. While just shy of record levels, 110 was reached on July 2, 3, 6 and 7. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual outside of a commercial building in Littletown. Heat was determined to be a contributing factor for 6 other individuals in Tucson. Three individuals who suffered from heart disease were found in their homes with A/C that had failed or was not on. Three others were found outdoors with complicating factors stemming from drug toxicity.

A thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph was measured at KDMA ASOS at 1634MST. A spotter recorded a gust to 68 mph near Speedway and Harrison at 1635MST and a gust to 63 mph was measured at KTUS ASOS at 1638MST.  In the Catalina Foothills from River/Swan to Skyline/Campbell numerous trees were downed, some of which fell on parking structures, vehicles and apartment buildings.  Around 7500 customers were without power due to 30 power poles being downed. Winds peeled parts of roofs off a handful of houses.

Thunderstorm winds caused extensive damage from the northeast to the south side of Tucson, from near Sabino High School southwestward to the Tucson International Airport. At least 40 power poles were downed or damaged, dozens of large trees were downed or uprooted, and several homes had portions of roofs peeled off by the winds.  Apartment complexes near Broadway and Camino Seco and 22nd and Kolb were especially hard hit as falling trees damaged a number of units, car shelters, and vehicles. Just south of this area along Golf Links Rd between Kolb and Wilmot and on Davis-Monthan AFB, numerous power poles were downed or damaged. Around 50,000 customers lost power as a result of the storms. A wind gusts to 62 mph was recorded at KDMA ASOS at 1818MST and 64 mph at KTUS ASOS at 1825MST.

Thunderstorm winds downed trees, power poles and caused structural damage from midtown to Tucson's southwest side. Downed trees damaged car shelters near Glenn and Alvernon and a house in Winterhaven. An exotic animal farm near I-10 and Wetmore sustained major damage to its shelters and fencing. Sporadic, mainly minor, wind damage  also occurred near Valencia and Camino Verde.
Thunderstorm winds downed at least 3 power poles along Mission Rd. south of Campus Dr.
At 1845MST, thunderstorm wind gusts to 59 mph were measured near Prospect and Larkspur CW8733 and near Old Spanish Trail and Melpomene Way FW3746.

A swath of large hail from 1 to 1.5 inches in diameter fell from near the Tucson Airport northwest to the campus of the University of Arizona, including at the NWS Tucson WFO. Hail damaged cars, skylights and roofs, including the roof at Rivera Elementary School.
A thunderstorm wind gust to 62 mph was measured at the Sasabe RAWS site.

Hot temperatures up to 6 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in eastern Pima County where temperatures topped out between 101 and 107 degrees.  A total of 14 heat-related fatalities were reported by the Pima County Medical Examiner. Heat was determined to be the primary cause of death for two individuals found in the desert, one near Three Points on the 12th and another in the Ironwood Forest National Monument on the 13th. Heat was also found to the primary cause of death for four individuals in Tucson. Two individuals were found on the 13th on Tucson streets and subsequently died at the hospital. Another was found deceased outdoors on the 13th and a fourth died on the 12th in their home where the A/C had been turned off. Heat was found to be a contributing factor in the deaths of 8 individuals in Tucson. Two persons died in their homes in which the A/C unit was either broken or turned off. They both also had complicating factors of heart disease. Six others were found outside at various locations in the city. The complicating factor for four of them was drug toxicity, while the other two suffered from other health issues.
Strong winds downed power lines near Interstate 19 and Pima Mine Road south of Tucson, causing a closure of the northbound lanes for more than 2 hours.

Hot temperatures 2 to 6 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in Tucson where temperatures topped out between 101 and 105 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined heat to be the primary cause of death for four individuals in the Tucson Metro area (two indoors with A/C units turned off and two others outdoors). Heat was determined to be a contributing factor in the deaths of five other individuals (two indoors with nonfunctioning A/C units but complicating factors of other health issues; one in a vehicle with other health issues; and two outdoors with complicating factors of drug toxicity).

Hot temperatures about 5 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in Tucson where temperatures topped out at 105 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined heat to be a contributing factor in the death of one individual found outside a commercial building in Tucson. A complicating factor in the fatality was drug toxicity.

Thunderstorm winds in Ajo downed four power poles and blew the roofs of a couple of houses while a number of other residences experienced minor roof damage along with damage to siding, garage doors, sheds and trees.

Very hot temperatures of 9 to 14 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across western and central Pima County the first seven days of July. Record highs of 113 degrees on July 1 and 110 on July 6 occurred at Ajo, but the hottest temperature was 114 on July 3. Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument topped at 109 degrees on July 3 and 5 and Sells reached 108 on July 1 and 3.

Hot temperatures around 6 degrees above normal, near 105 degrees, caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached across the Tucson Metro area August 25. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was a contributing factor in the death of one individual found indoors with a nonfunctioning AC unit. A complicating factor in this fatality was additional health issues.
Thunderstorm winds downed 400 saguaro cacti and damaged 800 others at Saguaro National Park West.
Thunderstorm winds downed trees at Cortaro and Silverbell.
Heavy rain of 1-1.5 in less than 1 hour caused Roger Wash to flow rapidly across Silverbell Rd. between West Hills of Gold and Sweetwater Drives.

Very hot temperatures 4 to 6 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across western Pima County. The low temperature at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument was 85 degrees and the high was 110. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was the primary cause of death for one individual found in the desert near Lukeville.

Very hot temperatures around 9 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across eastern Pima County. The low temperature at the Tucson International Airport was 84 degrees and the high was 108. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was the primary cause of death for two individuals  in Tucson. Heat was determined to be a contributing factor in the deaths of two others (one outdoors who had a complicating factor of drug toxicity; and an elderly individual in a vehicle who had other health issues).

Very hot temperatures of 7 to 13 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across western Pima County and the Tohono O'odham Nation August 26-29. Record highs at Ajo were 114, 115, 118 and 116 degrees, respectively. Record highs at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument included 114 degrees on August 28 and 113 on the 29th. Record highs at Sells included 108 degrees on August 26 and 27, and 109 on the 28th. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was the primary cause of death for two individuals found in the desert on the 26th in the Sells and Topawa areas.

A prolonged rain event on Jan 15 and 16 produced 1 to 3 inches of rain across the Tucson Metro area and adjacent foothills. Rising waters caused the closure of numerous roads at  low water crossings. Water rescues from flowing channels occurred including one in Arroyo Chico near Kino Parkway and another in the Santa Cruz River near Prince Rd. About 300 campers were stranded in Catalina St. Park when their egress from the park was cut off by flood waters.

Thunderstorm winds partially removed a roof near Irvington and Mission Rds. Winds then caused more extensive damage along Bilby and Valencia Roads between Camino De La Tierra and Camino De La Oeste, where 36 power poles were downed, one mobile home was rolled over, and several others lost roofs. Farther south, the Pascua Yaqui Fire Station truck bay sustained minor damage.
Two NWS employees reported quarter size hail on Tucson's east side.

Hot temperatures up to 5 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in Tucson where temperatures topped out between 100 and 105 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined heat to be the primary cause of death for seven individuals in the Tucson Metro area (six indoors with nonfunctioning A/C units and one hiking outdoors). Heat was determined to be a contributing factor in the deaths of three other individuals (two indoors with nonfunctioning A/C units but complicating factors of drug toxicity; and another outdoors with a complicating factor of other health issues).

Hot temperatures around 5 degrees above normal caused the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached in Tucson where temperatures topped out between 101 and 104 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined heat to be a contributing factor in the deaths of two individuals (one indoors with a nonfunctioning A/C unit and another outdoors). Both had complicating factors of drug toxicity.

Thunderstorm winds downed multiple trees in Oro Valley in an area generally bounded by Tangerine and 1st Avenue on the northeast to La Canada and Lambert Rd. Solar panels were damaged at Naranja Park and several Town Hall buildings sustained damage to roof tiles. Four windows and two sliding glass doors were blown out at one home.

Very hot temperatures up to 10 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across western Pima County and southern Pinal County August 4-6. A record high of 107 degrees occurred at San Manuel on August 5. Other high temperatures included 112 at Ajo on August 4 and 5; 110 at Picacho Peak on all three days; and 109 at Ajo on August 4.

Very hot temperatures of 5 to 12 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across western Pima County July 14-29. Record highs at Ajo included 118 degrees on July 25; 117 on July 21 and 22; 116 on July 18 and 19; 115 on July 14, 24 and 29; and 114 on the 15th. Record highs at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument were 114 degrees on July 20 and 23; and 112 on July 18, 19, 24 and 25. The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that heat was the primary cause of death for two individuals found in the desert at Organ Pipe Cactus NM on July 15 and 18 and another at Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge July 29. Heat was determined to be a contributing factor for one individual found in a driveway in Ajo on July 28. A complicating factor in the fatality was alcohol and drug intoxication.
Thunderstorm winds damaged the roofs of two homes in Topawa.

Thunderstorm winds caused extensive damage to the Fitness Center at the Pima Community College Desert Vista campus. Several trees were downed in Oro Valley. A wind gust to 60 mph was measured at the KAVQ AWOS at 1745MST.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole near Santa Rosa.
Around 1.5 of rain in less than 1 hour caused flash flooding of roadways in the Catalina Foothills of Tucson from Sunrise and Swan to River and Alvernon.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near Stella and Pantano in east Tucson.
Thunderstorm winds downed two power poles near Miller Ranch Rd northeast of Vail.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 59 mph was measured at CWOP site CW8733 in far northeast Tucson at 2025MST.

Thunderstorms winds downed power poles near Emigh and Sandario Rds. At nearby Marana High School, trees and saguaros were downed, solar paneled parking covers were heavily damaged, and one building sustained minor roof damage. At the athletic facilities, fences were damaged and the football field turf was rolled up by the wind and damaged. Classes were not held the next day due to a power outage and debris cleanup. Elsewhere, power poles were downed near Twin Peaks and Silverbell Roads and an empty tractor-trailer was overturned near Avra Valley and Sandario Roads. A wind gust to 64 mph was recorded at the KAVQ AWOS at 1535MST.

Very hot temperatures of 6 to 13 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across eastern Pima County July 14-29. Record highs at Tucson International Airport included 112 degrees on July 20 and 25 (also reached 112 July  18-19); 111 on July 16, 17 and 21; and 110 on the 15th. A total of 40 heat-related fatalities were reported by the Pima County Medical Examiner. Heat was determined to be the primary cause of death for 13 individuals in Tucson, one in Oro Valley, and one near Sahuarita. Seven of these deaths occurred outdoors while eight individuals were found indoors with A/C units which were either not working, turned off or not present at all. Heat was determined to be a contributing factor for 25 individuals, in Tucson or the immediate vicinity. Twelve of these included the complicating factor of drug toxicity (10 outdoors and 2 indoors with a nonfunctioning A/C). Ten in Tucson suffered from various health issues (2 outdoors and 8 indoors with a nonfunctioning A/C). Heat was a contributing factor for an additional three individuals who had other health issues, one each in Green Valley, Sahuarita and Vail.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole and a tree at the Tucson International Airport. A thunderstorm wind gust to 58 mph was measured at KTUS ASOS at 1752MST.
A thunderstorm wind gust to 72 mph was recorded at KAVQ AWOS at 1935MST.
Heavy rain of 1-1.5 in less than one hour caused Robb Wash to flow 2-3 feet deep across Pima Rd.
Thunderstorm winds downed a shallow-rooted tree which fell onto a mobile home, causing significant roof and wall damage.

Very hot temperatures of 8 to 11 degrees above normal caused the Major Heat Risk category to be reached across the Tucson Metro area August 4-6.
